Ambiguity 
• No general techniques for handling ambiguity
• Impossible to convert an ambiguous grammar to an unambiguous one 
automatically.
• Used with care, ambiguity can simplify the grammar
 
– Sometimes allows more natural definitions
 
– We need disambiguation mechanisms 
47
CFG → Derivation → Parse Tree → Check Ambiguity

Precedence and Associativity Declarations 
48
Ex: E → E + E | E * E | (E) | id
Ambiguity: Does a + b * c parse as (a + b) * c or a + (b * c)?
•
To fix ambiguity, one approach is to rewrite the grammar to enforce precedence (priority):
E → E + T | T
T → T * F | F
F → (E) | id
This works, but the grammar becomes more complex and less natural.
In compiler design, operator precedence and associativity are crucial for determining the order in which 
operations in an expression are evaluated.
∗has higher precedence than +

Contd.,
Alternative Approach (More Natural)
• Keep the natural grammar (even though it’s ambiguous).
• Use precedence and associativity declarations to disambiguate.
• Most tools allow precedence and associativity declarations to disambiguate grammars
49
E : E '+' E
  | E '*' E
  | '(' E ')'
  | id
  ;
Here In YACC::
•
%left '+' means + is left associative.
•
%left '*' means * is left associative and (because it appears later) it 
has higher precedence than +.
Use:
%left '+'
%left '*’
%%

Diagram showing two approaches to resolving ambiguity in grammar:
•
Grammar Rewriting (structuring E, T, F)
•
Disambiguating Declarations (%left, %right, precedence)
Both lead to the correct parse: a + (b * c)

Associativity Declarations 
• Consider the grammar E → E + E | int
• Ambiguous: two parse trees of int + int + int 
• Left associativity declaration: %left + 
51
Associativity defines the evaluation order for operators with 
the same precedence.
(int+int)+int
int+(int+int)​ 
Why is Associativity Needed? a−b−c
If: %right '-’ then: a-(b-c)
If: %left '-’ then: (a-b)-c

Precedence Declarations 
• Consider the grammar E → E + E | E * E | int
 
– And the string int + int * int 
52
1) 5 - 3 - 1
Ambiguity: is it (5 - 3) - 1 or 5 - (3 - 1)?
2) 2 + 3 * 4
Ambiguity: (+ (*)) vs (* (+))
3) a ^ b ^ c (exponentiation)
Ambiguity: (a ^ b) ^ c vs a ^ (b ^ c)
Precedence dictates which operator is evaluated first when 
multiple operators with different priorities are present.

Error Handling 
• Purpose of the compiler is
 
– To detect non-valid programs
 
– To translate the valid ones
• Many kinds of possible errors (e.g. in C)

Syntax Error Handling 
• When a compiler encounters an error in the source program, it must detect, report, and, if possible, 
recover from it without stopping compilation completely.
• Error handler should
 
– Report errors accurately and clearly
• Error messages should be informative (line number, nature of error).
• Example: instead of just "Syntax error", say "Missing semicolon '}' before at line 12".
 
– Recover from an error quickly
• The compiler should attempt to skip or fix the error and continue parsing.
• Prevents cascading errors (one mistake causing many false error reports).
 
– Not slow down compilation of valid code
• Error handling must not add overhead when code is correct.
• Normal compilation speed should be preserved.
• Good error handling is not easy to achieve 
54

Approaches to Syntax Error Recovery 
• From simple to complex
 
– Panic mode
 
– Error productions
 
– Automatic local or global correction
• Perform local corrections (insert, delete, replace tokens).
• Example: insert missing semicolon automatically.
• Theoretical method: change program minimally to make it syntactically correct.
• Too expensive, rarely used in practice.
• Not all are supported by all parser generators 
55

Error Recovery: Panic Mode 
• Simplest, most popular method
• When an error is detected:
 
– Discard tokens until one with a clear role is found (ex, ; or }).
 
– Continue from there
• Such tokens are called synchronizing tokens
 
– Typically, the statement or expression terminators 
56

Syntax Error Recovery: Panic Mode (Cont.) 
57
Panic Mode in YACC
special YACC terminal: error
This is not an ordinary token from the input program.
For example:
E → int
  | E + E
  | (E)
  | error int
  | (error)
The error symbol tells the parser how it can recover 
from certain syntax errors

Syntax Error Recovery: Error Productions 
• Idea: specify in the grammar the known common mistakes
• Essentially promotes common errors to alternative syntax
• Example:
 
– Written 5 x instead of 5 * x
 
– Add the production E → … | E E
• Disadvantage
 
– Complicates the grammar

Top-Down Parsing

Review of Parsing 
• Given a language L(G), a parser consumes a sequence of tokens s and produces a 
parse tree
• Issues:
 
– How do we recognize that s ∈ L(G) ?
 
– A parse tree of s describes how s ∈ L(G)
 
– Ambiguity: more than one parse tree (possible interpretation) for some 
string s
 
– Error: no parse tree for some string s
 
– How do we construct the parse tree? 
63

Abstract Syntax Trees 
• So far, a parser traces the derivation of a sequence of tokens
• The rest of the compiler needs a structural representation of the program
• Abstract syntax trees
 
– Like parse trees but ignore some details
 
– Abbreviated as AST 
64
E
              /     |     \
             E      +      E
             |             /|\
            int           ( E )
                          / | \
                         E  +  E
                         |       |
                        int   int
+
            / \
           5   +
              / \
             2   3

Example of Parse Tree 
• Traces the operation of the parser
• Captures the nesting structure
• But too much info
 
– Parentheses
 
– Single-successor nodes 
65
Why is the parse tree considered too detailed?
Parse tree represents the syntax according to the grammar. AST represents the essential structure of the 
program.

Example of Abstract Syntax Tree 
Here:
First PLUS = outer + 
Second PLUS = inner + 
5, 2, 3 = operands
66
How does the AST preserve the meaning?
The second + is inside the right subtree.
Therefore, the parentheses are no longer required.

Semantic Actions 
• This is what we’ll use to construct ASTs
• Each grammar symbol may have attributes
 
– An attribute is a property of a programming language construct
 
• Each production may have an action
 
– Written as: X → Y1 … Yn 
{ action }
 
– It tells the compiler what operation should be performed when this production is  processed.
67
For example:  E.val
The val attribute associated with non-terminal E.
For example: E → E₁ + E₂         { E.val = E₁.val + E₂.val }
The grammar tells us:  E → E₁ + E₂
and the semantic action tells us: Calculate the value of E

Semantic Actions: An Example 
68

Semantic Actions: An Example (Cont.) 
69

Semantic Actions: Dependencies 
• Semantic actions specify a system of equations
 
– Order of executing the actions is not specified 
70
E.val = 10
                /          \
          E₁.val=5       E₂.val=5
             │                    │
             5               E₃.val=5
                                /     \
                        E₄.val=2  E₅.val=3
                          │                  │
                         2                   3

syntax-directed translation: the dependency graph.
A dependency graph or directed graph is used to represent 
the flow of information and the order of evaluation among 
attributes within a parse tree.
Meaning of Red Boxes and Dashed Arrows:
•
Red boxes represent the operators and constants.
•
Dashed arrows indicate evaluation flow:
▪
For example, from E₁ we go to constant 5.
▪
From E₃ we go down to its + operator.
Why parentheses needed? Without parentheses, ambiguity arises in arithmetic grammar. Here, parentheses explicitly 
force evaluation order: 5+(2+3)=10.
